savePrompt.description: If true, the LLM prompt produced by the harness is included as a 'prompt' field on the action returned by core_harness, which causes it to be persisted in the episode replay. Defaults to false to keep replays small.

seed.description: Integer currently only used for selecting starting position.

strictMode.description: If true, agents must return only {'submission': int} (no extra fields like 'thoughts'), and per-agent TIMEOUT/ERROR/INVALID counts as a loss for the offending agent only — other agents win. If false (default), any agent error halts and voids the entire episode, matching the lenient research-mode behavior.

useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

openSpielGameName.description: Short name of the OpenSpiel game.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

action.thoughts:
The board is essentially empty with a single opponent (x) piece at the bottom of the center column (row 5, column 3). No threats or lines exist yet for either player. However, column 3 is the most strategically valuable position on the board due to the maximum number of possible winning lines (horizontal, vertical, and both diagonals) that pass through its squares.

If a move is made anywhere except column 3, the opponent can immediately respond by stacking directly on top of their own piece (at row 4, column 3). This would give them two adjacent pieces in the center column, creating an immediate positional advantage with multiple ways to build threats (including a potential vertical or diagonal force on their next turns).

By dropping in column 3 (on top of the x at row 4, column 3), this stacking is prevented. The opponent's center column is now interrupted by an o piece, and no vertical threat can be built there without further interference. This maintains balance in the center and keeps all of o's future options open without ceding early control. (Subsequent moves will depend on the opponent's response, but this is the only move that avoids an early disadvantage.)

Final Answer: 3

The board is nearly empty, with only two pieces placed in column 3 (x at the bottom row 5, o directly above it at row 4). This is x's second move overall. No immediate wins, blocks, or forced threats exist for either player, as each has too few pieces to reach 4-in-a-row.

The optimal strategy at this stage is to develop central control and connect pieces for future lines (horizontal, vertical, or diagonal). Placing in column 3 would stack x-o-x vertically, leaving x's pieces disconnected and permanently blocking a clean vertical win in that column due to o's intervening piece. This is suboptimal.

Instead, place adjacent to the existing x to form a connected base of two pieces. This is best achieved by dropping in column 2 (or symmetrically column 4), landing at row 5 column 2. This creates an immediate horizontal pair at the bottom and opens strong follow-up options for forks or longer lines. Columns 0, 1, 5, and 6 are inferior as they leave the new piece isolated from the existing x. Column 3 is avoided for the reasons above.

This move maintains balance and positions x for advantage in the midgame.

Final Answer: 2

The current board position has X pieces occupying the bottom row in columns 2 and 3, with O pieces stacked vertically in column 3 (rows 3 and 4). No player has an immediate win available. 

Playing in column 4 drops an X into the bottom row, creating three consecutive X pieces horizontally along row 5 (columns 2-4). This move generates two independent winning threats on the following turn: an X in column 1 (completing columns 1-4) or column 5 (completing columns 2-5). O can block at most one of these spots on their turn. 

O cannot win on their immediate turn (only two O pieces exist, so adding one yields at most three in a line). Even if O creates their own single threat (e.g., by extending vertically in column 3), I can ignore it and complete my horizontal four-in-a-row to win first. 

This is a forced win in two moves. (Column 1 achieves an equivalent fork with threats in columns 0 and 4, but column 4 is selected as the move here.)

Final Answer: 4
